newsitem.title: QATAR: Qatar emir steers oil state on road to revival.
newsitem.headline: Qatar emir steers oil state on road to revival.

text.p: Two years after seizing power, Qatar's Emir Sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa al-Thani has pursued bold policies steering his tiny but wealthy state towards political, economic and social revival, diplomats and economists say.
Sheikh Hamad, 47, ousted his father in a bloodless coup on June 27, 1995.

He has shown an independent mind on foreign and domestic policies -- he set up trade links with Israel, improved ties with Iran and Iraq, introduced women in government and decreed the Gulf's first municipal elections.

He has said he is determined to host a Middle East and North Africa economic summit to which Israel would be invited, despite Arab criticism of holding the meeting at a time when they see Israeli policies stalling the peace process.
He was outspoken this month when urging Washington during a visit to adopt more relaxed policies towards Iran and Iraq and said he disagreed with the Gulf state's main ally on that issue.

"He is following a well-crafted, pragmatic and independent policy -- even maverick -- which at times puts him at odds with the neighbours but that also wins him friends and admirers at home and abroad," one Western diplomat in Doha said.
Qatari citizens admire Sheikh Hamad's policies and say he has no opposition at home.

Sheikh Hamad's first year in office was marred by turbulence -- a failed coup alleged to have been masterminded by his father's aides, tensions with neighbouring states and his father's determined bid to regain the throne.
But as he completes his second year on Friday, he is seen to have weathered all storms and consolidated his power.
"People are happy with his domestic and economic policies and see the place booming," one longtime resident said.
Qatar's wealth and small population make it one of the world's richest states in terms of per capita income of $22,000.
"He is doing wonders on the economic front," a banker said.

His deposed father, Sheikh Khalifa bin Hamad al-Thani, was alleged to have siphoned off an estimated $3 billion to $7 billion of the state treasury to his personal accounts abroad. But in January, father and son reconciled and some of the money is believed to have been returned.

"There was a yawning budget deficit, mounting arrears to contractors and problems in paying wages to government staff. Qatar had to borrow twice to meet a balance of payments deficit and raise domestic loans to pay wages," the Qatari banker said.
"But now the country is flush with money and business is booming," he added.
Luxury villas, commercial centres and new roads are sprouting and changing the landscape of Doha at a dizzy pace. Most contractors say their order books are full for the next two years.
Bankers say much of the money comes from foreign investors lured by projects launched by the emir -- particularly in oil, gas and petrochemicals -- which has invigorated local liquidity.

"Bring your money and technology, we'll give you subsidised or even free local infrastructure and hospitality and tax breaks and take a major share in the equity and output," said another banker of Sheikh Hamad's policies to attract investment.
The emir said recently that investments by U.S. companies rose to $5.5 billion from $100 million two years ago. A further $10 billion came from Japanese, French and other European firms.

Qatar sits on about 500 trillion cubic feet (14 trillion cubic metres) of natural gas -- much of it in the world's largest offshore reservoir, the North Field. Its liquefied natural gas projects are expected to multiply its wealth.
Like other Gulf Arab states, Qatar remains essentially a family concern. The ruling al-Thani family has about 8,000 members and 11 of the emir's 18 cabinet ministers are al-Thanis.
But the emir does not hide his belief in democracy.

"If you do not allow the people to participate in government, you are only creating problems for yourself," he said in a recent interview. He said municipal elections due in November would be a first step towards other similar moves.
